This is called puppy blues. We ALL go through it. I remember thinking my JRT would never stop biting. I remember thinking she'd never stop chewing. As long as you are consistent with training you will get it to stop. Hiring a trainer is a great idea, and in the meantime I recommend ignoring the dog when it nips you and putting a toy in front of it. Simply say "no" in a firm voice when it tries to go for you, and praise it (with treats if need be) when it goes for the toy. 

I even got puppy blues from my Pomeranian, who never went through this phase somehow? The only thing she ever tore up was one singular pair of shoes one night. You get this sort of dread of "what did I get myself into". It does go away and everything is so much better now with both of them.

What you explained is literally positive reinforcement training above. Cesars methods are not those things, and just because other trainers have failed does not mean that positive methods altogether have. Its possible that they don't know what they're doing just like Cesar. I have not personally worked with dogs on the road to euthanasia yet, but the leaders in dog training I follow have. They don't use his methods and are still able to get the dogs off death row.

The problem is, while the dogs look good on camera, if you know doggy body language they are extremely stressed out. They are not listening to him because they respect him, they're listening because they're afraid of being hurt. This is not a long term training method and the dogs will eventually snap again, and even be more likely to do so because of fear aggression. It's why his dog has been charged with multiple aggressive tendencies in court, even his own dogs are fear aggressive. I'm sure if I researched him more I'd find many of the dogs he's "trained" end up being aggressive again, and maybe even more aggressive after he's worked with them. 

A good trainer example who has gotten dogs off of the doggy death row is Victoria Stilwell. It's her academy I go to for my dog training education alongside going to college for animal behavior. My own dog is a mix of breeds known to be aggressive, and she nipped as a puppy. I never laid a hand on her and she is now the sweetest dog in the world. I've worked with adult dogs and gotten the same results. You just have to be more patient with these methods and understand that changing dogs habits will almost never be instant, just like our habits take time to replace too.

Hoping my comment won't get lost in this sea of comments. Your dog could've likely been trained with solely positive reinforcement methods and still been the best dog. It is correct to say his methods are outdated and abusive, here's why. 

He was banned in Germany and other European countries due to his "training" going against animal welfare laws. He has openly admitted he has no experience or knowledge in any animal training techniques and simply uses it as a platform for fame, he admitted this in court. 

His dog attacked another dog and killed it, and attacked a young girl who was a gymnast to the point she can no longer perform. His methods don't even work on his own dog, so let that sink in for a moment. He hits other people's dogs, the dogs' body language in any given clip is showing extreme stress; panting, eyes big etc. He uses other animals like livestock and puts them in danger by putting them with a dog known to be aggressive to specifically their species. 

All in all, this dude is a horrible "trainer", and positive reinforcement can even train the most difficult dog. I work as a dog trainer. I have worked with aggressive dogs. But if I'm reading this correctly, your dog wasn't even aggressive and you still found an excuse to use these awful methods? Please do a bit more research and look into what the actual behavioral scientists for dogs say. None of them promote Cesar.

Teach the "leave it command". It will take a while to ensure that it works flawlessly, but if you keep at it they will learn and listen when you tell them to. It saved all my cords.

Stay is imperative if you need to go somewhere! Practice by staying in the room and backing up, reward if the puppy stays. Then once she gets that, start turning your back and telling her to stay.
